extracted.intended_audience: Researchers and practitioners serving as ICLR 2026 peer reviewers (machine learning conference reviewers)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluation criteria for reviewers assessing submissions to ICLR 2026, including required procedures (CoE, LLM disclosure), what to evaluate in papers, how to write reviews, and how to participate in discussions and meetings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timeliness and substantive reviews
rubrics_metrics.description: Your reviews are timely and substantive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Timely, high quality reviews are essential. Main reviewer tasks include writing reviews within specified windows and participating in discussions. Penalties for late or poor-quality reviews include loss of access to reviews of your own papers during rebuttal, warnings from ACs/SACs, and potential desk rejection of your own submissions if you fail to remediate low-quality reviews.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adherence to Code of Ethics and Code of Conduct
rubrics_metrics.description: All reviewers are required to read and adhere to the ICLR Code of Ethics and Code of Conduct. Reviewers are asked to raise potential violations as part of the review process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Code of Ethics applies to submission, reviewing, and discussion. Authors are encouraged to discuss potential ethics issues in their submission (this discussion does not count against page limits). If you identify a potential CoE violation, indicate it in the CoE report; ACs will work with PCs and the ethics board. Read the CoE before starting reviews since the CoE report is a required form when submitting your review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclosure of LLM usage (reviewers and authors)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of LLMs is allowed as a writing assistance tool, but reviewers (and authors) must disclose any significant usage. Reviewers take full responsibility for content written under their name, including LLM-generated content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The review form will include a field to specify how you used LLMs. Failures to disclose LLM usage may result in reviews being flagged as low quality and could put the reviewer's papers at risk for desk rejection. If authors disclose significant LLM usage or if undisclosed usage is uncovered during discussion, notify the area chair.

rubrics_metrics.name: Careful reading and literature checking
rubrics_metrics.description: Read the paper carefully and give yourself sufficient time; look up related work and citations to comprehensively evaluate the submission.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While reading, consult the references and related work to judge motivation and novelty. Consider supplementary material if it helps answer questions that arise from the main paper before asking authors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider the objective of the work
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify the paper's goal: addressing a known application/problem, drawing attention to a new application/problem, or introducing/explaining a new theoretical finding (or combination).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Different objectives require different considerations when judging potential value and impact. Tailor your evaluation to the stated objective of the submission.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify and report strong points
rubrics_metrics.description: Document what the submission does well (clarity, technical correctness, experimental rigor, reproducibility, novel findings).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be positive and constructive in the summary. Explicitly list strengths so authors (and ACs) understand the paper's merits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify and report weak points
rubrics_metrics.description: Document weaknesses across clarity, correctness, experiments, novelty, assumptions, and other aspects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be comprehensive when listing weak points. Distinguish between serious flaws that affect acceptance and minor issues intended to help authors improve their presentation or experiments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be mindful of biases and community value
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid biased judgments; consider value and interest for the entire ICLR community, not only your own tastes or niche interests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep an open mind about papers that may be outside your immediate preferences but still valuable to practitioners, theorists, or other subcommunities.

rubrics_metrics.name: What is the specific question or problem tackled?
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine the precise research question or problem the paper addresses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the problem is clearly stated and whether it is a meaningful question for the community.

rubrics_metrics.name: Is the approach well motivated and well-placed in the literature?
rubrics_metrics.description: Judge whether the proposed approach is motivated and appropriately situated relative to prior work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check that the paper explains why the approach is needed compared to related methods, and that citations and comparisons are appropriate given contemporaneous work policies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do the results support the claims (correctness and rigor)?
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine if theoretical or empirical results are correct and scientifically rigorous; check assumptions and derivations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For theoretical work, check proofs, stated assumptions, and clarity about what is novel. For empirical work, verify experimental design, statistical significance, reproducibility, and whether results substantiate claims. Ask for clarifications when steps in proofs or experimental setup are unclear.

rubrics_metrics.name: What is the significance of the work?
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess whether the submission contributes new knowledge and sufficient value to the ICLR community.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Significance does not require state-of-the-art results. Value can be empirical, theoretical, or practical. Judge impact on the community and whether the contribution convincingly demonstrates novelty or utility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Initial review structure and required components
rubrics_metrics.description: Organize the initial review: summarize claims, list strengths and weaknesses, clearly state initial recommendation with one or two key reasons, provide supporting arguments, ask clarifying questions, and give additional feedback to improve the paper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be constructive and make it clear which points are for improving the paper versus those driving your accept/reject decision. Provide specific evidence and actionable suggestions. Include questions you want authors to answer in the rebuttal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complete the Code of Ethics (CoE) report
rubrics_metrics.description: When submitting your review, complete a CoE report with two questions: whether there is a potential CoE violation, and (if yes) an explanation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Read the CoE before reviewing so you can accurately answer the report. For suspected CoE violations, indicate them in the CoE report; the AC will coordinate with PCs and the ethics board.

rubrics_metrics.name: Engage in discussion and be open to changing your rating
rubrics_metrics.description: Actively participate in asynchronous discussion with authors, other reviewers, and ACs; be open to modifying your initial recommendation based on new information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain a spirit of openness. Update your review after discussion and any author revisions; state reasoning for changes (what did/didn't change your recommendation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Participate in borderline paper meetings
rubrics_metrics.description: Attend (virtually) area-chair facilitated meetings for borderline papers when scheduled, and familiarize yourself with other reviewers' feedback prior to the meeting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ACs will schedule and facilitate these meetings. Attendance is expected unless there is an emergency; information from reviewers who miss the meeting may be leveraged by ACs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide a final recommendation with updated reasoning
rubrics_metrics.description: After discussions and any virtual meetings, provide a final recommendation to the area chair and explain what changed and why.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Finalize your review after considering author responses and additional evidence. Be explicit about how your view shifted (if at all) and what influenced that shift.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of supplementary material
rubrics_metrics.description: Supplementary material is optional to read; it can often answer questions that arise from the main paper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You are not required to read supplementary material, but consider consulting it before asking authors for clarifications that may already be provided there.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requesting additional experiments (scope constraints)
rubrics_metrics.description: You may ask for additional experiments, but they should not significantly change the content of the submission; they should be limited in scope and serve to more thoroughly validate existing results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid requests that would require the authors to substantially change the paper's contributions or add new directions. Frame experiment requests as narrowly as possible to test existing claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: State-of-the-art results are not mandatory
rubrics_metrics.description: A submission's lack of state-of-the-art performance is not alone grounds for rejection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the paper convincingly demonstrates new, relevant, impactful knowledge. Papers can bring value via empirical insights, theory, methods for practitioners, etc., without beating SOTA.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contemporaneous work and arXiv comparison policy
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors are not required to compare to contemporaneous peer-reviewed work published within two months of the deadline; arXiv is not considered peer-reviewed, so comparisons to arXiv-only papers are not required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contemporaneous definition: papers published (peer-reviewed venue) on or after July 24, 2025 relative to a Sept 24 deadline. While not required, authors are strongly encouraged to cite related contemporaneous or arXiv work if aware of it; reviewers can bring such work to authors' attention but lack of comparison cannot be basis for rejection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling non-CoE policy violations
rubrics_metrics.description: To discuss other policy violations (e.g., plagiarism, double submission, paper length, formatting), contact the AC/SAC or PC as appropriate via confidential comment with readership restrictions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For CoE-related issues use the CoE report. For other violations, use confidential communication channels so ACs/PCs can investigate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluation criteria exemplified in accept-leaning review example
rubrics_metrics.description: Exemplar criteria that support leaning-to-accept: significant algorithmic or theoretical contribution, clear explanation of contributions, plausible novelty, reasonable empirical support across domains, and willingness to clarify minor theoretical/experimental points.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The sample review praises clarity of contribution, notes where theory/experiments need clarification (e.g., assumptions, parameter choices, computational cost), and indicates willingness to increase score after satisfactory clarifications in author response. Use such balanced critiques that separate fixable issues from fundamental flaws.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluation criteria exemplified in reject-leaning review example
rubrics_metrics.description: Exemplar criteria that support leaning-to-reject: failure to demonstrate the existence of the claimed problem, poorly justified algorithm, lack of evidence for correctness, insufficient or unclear experiments (missing details, lack of statistical significance, poor baselines/tuning), imprecise writing, and unsupported overclaims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The sample review lists concrete experimental and presentation deficiencies to justify rejection (e.g., missing experiment details, inadequate tuning of baselines, unclear assumptions, inconsistent notation). Use these concrete checks when judging whether evidence supports claims.
